title: Subhuti weeps (section 14)
hookLine: hearing it, Subhuti weeps; the Buddha recalls being cut apart by a king without anger, because he had no idea of a self

cards: So far in this sutra, Subhuti has been the steady one: calm, exact, the student with the careful answer. The Buddha has praised him for dwelling in peace.
Then, at the start of section fourteen, the text says he hears this teaching, understands its meaning deeply, and weeps. Tears, from the one praised for his peace.
He speaks through them, and the Buddha answers with a memory from very long ago.

teach.b: First, the tears. Since he gained the eye of wisdom, Subhuti says, he has never heard a teaching like this.
Someone who hears it with a clear, trusting mind will see things as they truly are, and that is rare and wonderful. Second, rare in a later age.
He's been taught directly, so trusting it isn't hard for him, he says; but someone in a later time who hears this and trusts it will be rare.
The Buddha agrees, and adds: anyone who hears this and isn't startled, isn't frightened, isn't afraid, is rare indeed. Third, the memory.
Long ago, the Buddha says, a king cut his body apart, limb from limb. At that time he had no idea of a self, a person, a being, a life. If he had, anger and ill will would have risen in him.
They didn't. He calls this the perfection of patience, and then, in the sutra's way, says it is not the perfection of patience. Fourth, why the tears?
The sutra doesn't explain them. Some readers hear joy, the relief of finally hearing it said. Some hear grief for how long it took.
Some hear both. The text simply lets him weep, and keeps going.

teach.h: WHY THE TEARS? THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY.
teach.b: And the memory beside the tears isn't a lesson in pretending a wound doesn't hurt.
It's a claim about where anger comes from: the idea of a self that has been wronged. That's an extreme story, told about a Buddha.
Everyday hurts are smaller, a remark, a slight at work, and the same question can still be asked of them, gently.

how: Mahayana Buddhists count patience among the perfections of a bodhisattva, and teachers tell the story of the sage of patience and the king alongside this section.

o: a ritual of weeping that monks perform at sutra readings
Subhuti's tears on hearing and deeply understanding this teaching
Subhuti's grief when the Buddha scolds him for doubting

p: no idea of a self, so no anger
is not the perfection of patience

s: the sutra explains exactly why Subhuti weeps
it doesn't. readers hear joy, grief, or both; the text lets him weep.
the Buddha says anger would have arisen if he'd held an idea of a self
he had no such idea, and so no anger or ill will.
Subhuti says this teaching is easy for anyone to trust
trusting it is not hard for him, he says, but one who trusts it in a later age will be rare. the Buddha adds that whoever isn't startled or afraid is rare indeed.

games.q: you're the sage in the Buddha's memory. a king is cutting your body apart. what does the story say happened in your mind?
o: anger, held back by sheer willpower.
no idea of a self, and so no anger.
games.why: he had no idea of a self, a person, a being or a life. if he had, the Buddha says, anger and ill will would have arisen.

practice: Bring to mind one small hurt from this week or this month, not the biggest, and notice where the body holds it: the jaw, the chest, the shoulders.
Breathe into that place; you don't have to excuse what happened or decide it was fine, just notice the one inside who was hurt, and the story that keeps telling it.
Let the grip ease one breath's worth, and if it doesn't, that's all right.

wordCard.voice: Subhuti weeps. Hearing the sutra and understanding it deeply, Subhuti weeps; the Buddha recalls being cut apart without anger, because he held no idea of a self. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: patience, forbearance; the perfection the Buddha names in this section.

carryVoice: Your line: he wept to hear it. Even the steady one was moved. Gently, then, until tomorrow.
